articles.title: What to back up (and watch) when you self-host a crypto payment gateway
articles.excerpt: Most self-hosting advice about backups boils down to "dump the database somewhere". For a crypto payment gateway that's necessary, but it isn't the whole story, and the parts people skip are the ones…
articles.body: Most self-hosting advice about backups boils down to "dump the database somewhere". For a crypto payment gateway that's necessary, but it isn't the whole story, and the parts people skip are the ones that hurt. Here's the thing that took me a while to see clearly: on a non-custodial gateway, a dead server doesn't lose you money. The money was never on it. What a dead server loses you is the ability to prove what happened : which order a deposit belonged to, which webhooks fired, whether that $499 payment from Tuesday ever confirmed. And if you lose the wrong file, you also lose every two-factor secret and webhook secret your install ever issued. This post is the backup and monitoring setup I'd put on any Coldtill server before it takes a real payment.
articles.author: Coldtill

articles.body: Microsoft Security Research published a short, numbers-heavy analysis on 2 November 2026 of which vulnerabilities attackers actually use. The headline figure: from 1999 through September 2026 roughly 383,000 vulnerabilities were disclosed, and only about 2,000 CVEs (around 0.5%) have been linked to real-world exploitation. The exploited set is 2,056 CVEs in their data. Fewer than 1 in 200 published CVEs ever gets used in an attack. This post goes through what the report says, what I think follows from it, and where the numbers need care. Everything quoted below comes from the Microsoft Security blog post , which I read in full.

articles.title: There's More to AI Than Just ChatGPT
articles.excerpt: When people talk about AI today, ChatGPT is usually the first thing that comes to mind. But the more I explore this field, the more I realise that there's a lot happening behind these tools that we ra…
articles.body: When people talk about AI today, ChatGPT is usually the first thing that comes to mind. But the more I explore this field, the more I realise that there's a lot happening behind these tools that we rarely talk about. I've been particularly interested in understanding how modern AI applications actually work, beyond simply writing prompts and getting responses. A few concepts have really caught my attention. LLMs: What's happening behind the responses? Language models do much more than simply repeat information. Understanding tokens, context and next-token prediction gives us a better idea of how these systems generate responses.

articles.title: Why Coating Recipes End Up Edited on a Process Engineer Workstation Instead of the Lab
articles.excerpt: A precision optics manufacturer made coated lenses for industrial and scientific instruments. A coating recipe is the set of parameters for a deposition run: layer materials, thickness targets, temper…
articles.body: A precision optics manufacturer made coated lenses for industrial and scientific instruments. A coating recipe is the set of parameters for a deposition run: layer materials, thickness targets, temperatures, and the sequence of steps inside the vacuum chamber. Recipes were supposed to live in the process system used on the factory floor, which records every revision and requires an approval before a change reaches a machine. In practice, engineers kept working copies as spreadsheets, because tweaking a sequence in a spreadsheet is quicker than opening a change request. During a customer audit, a reviewer asked which recipe version had produced a particular batch.
articles.author: nsecsoft nsecsoft

articles.title: What Does Durable Execution Guarantee, and Where Does It Stop?
articles.excerpt: Durable execution guarantees that a workflow's completed steps survive a crash and do not run again, so during a failure or restart, the workflow picks up from that last recorded step. It does not gua…
articles.body: Durable execution guarantees that a workflow's completed steps survive a crash and do not run again, so during a failure or restart, the workflow picks up from that last recorded step. It does not guarantee that a step runs exactly once and therefore it won't mitigate bad business logic. Think of a delivery company with ten packages to deliver that day. The driver successfully delivers four and records each one in their delivery log, but on the way to the fifth delivery, their vehicle breaks down. A replacement driver is dispatched to take over. They don't need to start from the first delivery; they know which four packages have already been delivered because it's in the log, and they can continue with the remaining six. In Dapr Workflow, that log is the workflow history.
articles.author: Joni Collinge

articles.title: Unconstrained Kerberos Delegation Leaves a Reusable Ticket Trail
articles.excerpt: Unconstrained Kerberos Delegation Leaves a Reusable Ticket Trail Kerberos delegation exists to let a service act for a user against another service. Constrained delegation narrows that authority to na…
articles.body: Unconstrained Kerberos Delegation Leaves a Reusable Ticket Trail Kerberos delegation exists to let a service act for a user against another service. Constrained delegation narrows that authority to named services. Unconstrained delegation is broader: a service trusted this way can receive a forwarded ticket-granting ticket and use it to reach services beyond the immediate request. That design makes every unconstrained endpoint an attractive target. Microsoft's documentation and security guidance treat unconstrained delegation as a legacy and high-risk configuration. The Windows Server Kerberos troubleshooting material describes scenarios in which it is used, while Microsoft's Active Directory hardening guidance recommends moving away from it.
articles.author: kozhevniko

articles.title: Understanding Large Language Models (LLMs): What Happens Behind the Chat?
articles.excerpt: We've all probably had a conversation with an AI chatbot. We ask questions, request explanations, generate code, summarize documents, and sometimes even ask it to help us solve everyday problems. But…
articles.body: We've all probably had a conversation with an AI chatbot. We ask questions, request explanations, generate code, summarize documents, and sometimes even ask it to help us solve everyday problems. But have you ever stopped and wondered: How does an AI actually understand what we're saying and generate such human-like responses? As someone exploring the world of Artificial Intelligence and emerging technologies, this is one of the questions I wanted to understand better. So, let's explore one of the technologies behind modern AI chatbots: Large Language Models (LLMs). 1. What is a Large Language Model (LLM)? A Large Language Model, commonly known as an LLM, is an AI model trained on large amounts of text data to recognize language patterns and generate human-like text.

Apple and Google often talk about the strict guidelines that apps need to follow in order to be allowed on their stores. articles.body: Created by LeSean Thomas and Studio Mir, who both worked on The Legend of Korra , Bass X Machina is a reimagining of the story of Bass Reeves (Brian Tyree Henry), an escaped slave who worked in Indian Territory as a deputy U.S. Marshal. Reeves’ real life was extraordinary, and is said to have inspired the character of the Lone Ranger, but Bass X Machina also gives him a cybernetic arm that shoots magic bullets. The criminals he fights get even bigger upgrades, and the stakes can at times escalate to truly ludicrous levels. Henry does an especially great job expressing exasperation as Bass faces plenty of absurd foes, like an outlaw in a rampaging bull mech that requires complex cooperation to take down.

articles.body: Avatar: The Last Airbender has more than its fair share of heartfelt moments and poignant lines. Whether it’s Aang reassuring a downtrodden Toph in the vast loneliness of the desert, or Ursa’s parting words to her son Zuko before disappearing in the middle of the night, the series can be surprisingly deep for what some might (incorrectly) consider a mere children’s show. No character embodies that richness and depth more than Uncle Iroh, who begins as Zuko's wise mentor and becomes so much more. articles.title: James Webb Space Telescope uncovers new clues about the origins of 'interstellar invader' comet 3I/ATLAS
articles.excerpt: The findings are another clue towards understanding the origins of 3I/ATLAS and the planet-forming conditions around other stars.
articles.body: Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), scientists have found that the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS was built from tiny grains of ice mixed with dust that are quite different from the solar system’s comets. These ice grains do, however, bear striking similarities to some icy bodies located at the edge of the solar system, beyond the orbit of Neptune, so-called trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs). 3I/ATLAS was discovered entering the solar system in the summer of 2025. It was only the third object found entering the solar system from farther afield in the Milky Way after 1I/'Oumuamua , seen in 2017, and 2I/Borisov , detected in 2019. This meant the interstellar comet offered a rare chance to glimpse the conditions under which such bodies form in other star systems.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 2, 2000: Expedition 1 Arrives at the International Space Station
articles.excerpt: Expedition 1 crewmates Bill Shepherd, Yuri Gidzenko and Sergei Krikalev pose with a model of the space station as it appeared in 2000.
articles.body: On Nov. 2, 2000, the International Space Station welcomed its first long-term residents: NASA astronaut Bill Shepherd and two Russian cosmonauts, Yuri Gidzenko and Sergei Krikalev. The mission was called Expedition 1. Before this expedition, NASA had launched five, one-week-long Space Shuttle missions to help build the space station and bring up supplies. But this time, the crew would be staying for four and a half months, and they weren't taking the shuttle. Instead, they took a Russian Soyuz spacecraft , and this was the first Soyuz to ever dock at the space station. During their stay at the space station, they unpacked supplies and installed new equipment, including the first solar arrays.
